source_text:
Ἀναγνοὺς γὰρ, Ἔκλαυσαν καὶ ἐδεήθησάν μου· καὶ, Ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ ὢν, εὗρόν με, εἴποι
ἂν, ὅτι καὶ τὸ ἑξῆς οὖν ἐστιν, Ἐκεῖ ἐλαλήθη πρὸς αὐτούς· τουτέστι τοὺς κλαύσαντας
καὶ δεηθέντας, καὶ ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ ὢν, εὑρόντας τὸν Θεόν. Ἐκ παρατηρήσεως δὲ ὁμοίων
ῥητῶν καὶ τοῦτο ἀκολούθως εἰρῆσθαι δείξομεν. Ἐν τῇ Γενέσει ὁ Θεὸς τῷ Ἀδὰμ
ἐντολὴν διδοὺς, οὕτω φησίν· Ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ βρώσει φαγῇ·
ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρὸν, οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ· ᾗ δ' ἂν
ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε. Ἀρξάμενος γὰρ κἀκεῖ ἀπὸ ἑνικοῦ ἐν
τῷ εἰρηκέναι, παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ βρώσει φαγῇ, ἐπιφέρει
πληθυντικῶς, εἰπὼν, ἀπὸ δὲ τοῦ ξύλου τοῦ γινώσκειν καλὸν καὶ πονηρὸν, οὐ φάγεσθε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ· ᾗ δ' ἂν ἡμέρᾳ φάγητε ἀπ' αὐτοῦ, θανάτῳ ἀποθανεῖσθε. Ὅτε γὰρ
περὶ τῆς ἐντολῆς δι' ἧς αὐτὸν ἐν ζωῇ ταύτην τηροῦντα ἠθέλησεν εἶναι, ἑνικῶς
ἐντέλλεται, καὶ φησίν· Ἀπὸ παντὸς ξύλου τοῦ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ βρώσει φαγῇ.
thought_title: The singular after the plural in Hosea is deliberate, as Genesis shows
orientation: Origen is explaining why Hosea shifts from plural verbs to a singular, arguing that the apparent inconsistency is a deliberate scriptural pattern rather than a scribal error.
pass_a_gloss: For [someone] having read, "They wept and beseeched me," and, "Being in the house, they found me," would say that the next [part] then is, "There it was spoken to them"—that is, to the ones who wept and beseeched, and being in the house, found God. And from observation of similar sayings we will show that this too has been said consistently. In Genesis God, giving a command to Adam, says thus: "From every tree of the one in the paradise, for food you shall eat; but from the tree of the knowing good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die." For having begun there too from [the] singular in the saying, "from every tree of the one in the paradise, you shall eat," he brings in [the] plural, saying, "but from the tree of the knowing good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die." For when concerning the command through which he wanted him to be keeping this in life, he commands in [the] singular, and says: "From every tree of the one in the paradise, for food you shall eat."

choices.english: And from observation of similar sayings
choices.why: Keeps the noun 'observation' as the source does, rather than turning it into a verb, preserving the methodological tone.
The adverb 'consistently' captures the sense of following a pattern, not merely 'in sequence' or 'consequently'.
The participle is present, showing the action in progress as God speaks; 'giving' preserves this.
The dative 'βρώσει' is instrumental or modal, 'for food' or 'as food'; the future 'φαγῇ' is a command in the LXX idiom.

choices.english: and on whatever day you eat
choices.why: The indefinite relative with 'ἄν' plus subjunctive is a generalizing condition; 'whatever day' captures this.
rejected: and on the day you eat
and in whatever day you may eat

choices.why: The cognate dative plus future is a Hebraism; 'by death you shall die' preserves the emphatic doubling.

pass_b_english: After reading, “They wept and begged me,” and, “Being in the house, they found me,” someone might say that what follows is also, “There it was spoken to them.” That is, to those who wept and begged, and who, being in the house, found God. And from observation of similar sayings we will show that this too has been said consistently.

In Genesis, when God gives a command to Adam, God speaks like this: “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food; but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:16-17). For there too, having begun from the singular in saying, “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food,” God brings in the plural, saying, “But from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, you shall not eat from it; and on whatever day you eat from it, by death you shall die” (Genesis 2:17). For when it concerns the command through which God willed Adam to be in life by keeping it, he commands in the singular, and says, “From every tree in the garden you may eat as food” (Genesis 2:16).
